opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at that age I didn't see it as a big strategic decision. In Shanghai, if you're a kid who likes math, you naturally get pulled into the competition track. There are math olympiad classes, special programs, and a whole ecosystem around them. So my choices were shaped less by careful planning and more by what I enjoyed and what was in front of me.

There were roughly two paths. One was the regular one: study hard, take the gaokao, get into a good university. The other was competitions. If you did well enough you could get recommended to a top university, and you also got to spend your time on harder, more interesting problems. I leaned toward competitions mostly because I liked the feeling of being stuck on a problem and then suddenly seeing it. That was more fun than drilling exam questions.

Looking back, I think the real lesson was about environment. Being around people who were very strong and genuinely curious mattered more than any single choice. You'd see someone your age solve something in a way you'd never have thought of, and that pushes you. It also humbles you early, which I think is healthy.

I also didn't know then that I'd move from math to physics, and later to AI. At fifteen you think you're choosing a direction, but really you're choosing what kind of thinking you want to train. For me that was working from first principles and staying with a hard problem for a long time. That carried over much more than any specific subject did.

r001.rationale: The response says he leaned toward competitions because he enjoyed challenging problems, but it does not say he had never participated in competitions before or attribute his desire to that.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't think of them as "options" in a very deliberate way at the time. I grew up in Shanghai, and the path in front of me was pretty standard: do well on the zhongkao, get into a good high school, then try to get into a good university. What changed things for me was competition math and, later, informatics. I was decent at math, and someone suggested I try the olympiad track, and once I got into it I realized I liked problems that didn't have a textbook answer, where you had to sit with something for hours and build the solution yourself.

So around the time I was choosing a high school, the question became less "which school has the best overall reputation" and more "where can I actually keep doing this." I ended up in a place with a strong competition culture, and that mattered more than I understood then. The people around me were obsessed in a good way. We'd trade problems, argue about solutions, stay late. That environment taught me that being surrounded by people slightly better than you is the fastest way to grow, which is something I still believe about research.

In hindsight, the competition path also gave me a kind of freedom. If you do well enough, you get recommended into a university like Tsinghua without the full gaokao pressure, and that lets you spend your last year or two of high school actually learning things rather than drilling. I didn't plan it that carefully. I just followed what I found interesting, and I was lucky that it happened to also be a path that opened doors.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he was encouraged to try the olympiad track and then discovered he liked it, but does not say he strongly wanted competitions because he had never participated in them before.

astra-6.text: At that point, I didn’t have a clear idea of what I wanted to do in the long run. I was thinking more about the next step: which high school would give me a good environment to learn and keep my options open? Looking back, it’s easy to describe education as a deliberate path, but when you’re that age, you’re making decisions with a pretty limited understanding of what comes afterward.
